summary: Presents further design concepts for datalanguage, the language of CCA's datacomputer project. It gives preliminary results of the language design, a model for the semantics of data language, and notes on future considerations.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 610 presents preliminary ideas for datalanguage, the language used to request data services from CCA's datacomputer. It covers shared data, descriptions, retrieval, access controls and a model for testing language concepts, while noting that the design was not complete.

questions: how to share data across different computers
how did rfc 610 propose sharing database views
subtitle: Design concepts for a language used to request services from the datacomputer.

tldr.problem: CCA was designing a data-management utility for network users with different computers, languages and views of shared information.
tldr.mechanism: The proposed datalanguage would describe data and operations, support selective retrieval and updates, and let the datacomputer manage representation, access and processing choices.
tldr.outcome: RFC 610 presents preliminary design concepts and a model for exploring language semantics; it says the design was incomplete and syntax had not yet been proposed.

today: RFC 610 is a preliminary 1973 design paper; it says the datalanguage specification was still in development and that the design was incomplete.

sections.title: The Datacomputer and Its Language
sections.content:
The datacomputer was designed as a dedicated network system for storing and managing data for other computers. Datalanguage was the language used for all requests: describing and creating data, retrieving or changing it, and accessing services. The RFC says the datacomputer was intended to support data shared by programs on different hardware and operating systems.

This paper presents concepts and preliminary results from a second design iteration, not a finished specification. The authors say they expected users to first have access to the new language during 1975.
sections.plainLanguage: The datacomputer was a network service for storing and managing shared data. Datalanguage was the way other systems would describe data and request work from it.

sections.title: Sharing Data Across the Network
sections.content:
The authors identify data sharing as a central design issue. Different applications may need different views of the same database, and different computers may use different representations for values such as numbers and strings. Datalanguage was intended to let users describe their data and the view they needed without always depending on how the data was physically stored.

Because network transfer was limited, the authors emphasized selecting only the needed parts of a file. They also describe the datacomputer as one specialized participant among cooperating processes, where other systems could handle computation or user interaction. Access control, data integrity and descriptions of both logical meaning and physical representation were part of the design problem.
sections.plainLanguage: Different programs may need different views of shared data, even when it is stored once. The language was intended to describe what data a program needed so the datacomputer could select and transfer only the relevant parts.

sections.title: Data Types, Structures and Operations
sections.content:
The language concepts include basic items such as numbers, characters, booleans and bits, as well as aggregates such as structs, arrays, strings, lists and directories. A description records properties of data, including its name, type, size, representation and privacy information. Lists and directories can change as members are added or removed; a struct has a fixed set of named components.

The design also discusses operations for selecting sets of records, ordering data, validating values, controlling privacy, converting representations, and defining virtual or derived data. These are design concepts, not a complete syntax or final specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Datalanguage was planned to describe both simple values and larger structures such as lists and records. It also aimed to support search, validation, access control and conversions between data forms.

sections.title: A Model and Work Still to Do
sections.content:
The authors were developing a model datacomputer to explore semantics: it included data objects and descriptions, primitive functions, an interpreter and a compiler for a simple language. The model had enough primitives to express examples such as retrieving selected list members, but the authors call it embryonic.

Further work included data structures beyond hierarchical ones, access regulation, encryption, a process interaction protocol, language syntax and application support. The paper says syntax had not yet been proposed and describes the model as a way to refine the design before a detailed specification and staged implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: The team used a model program to test how data objects and language operations could work together. The language still needed a syntax and more work on access control, process communication and application needs.
